<reason>PRO (Side B) built the cleaner route to victory around the coordination problem: the harm is collective, so the child whose parents say no is exiled under any parental-control or design regime, and only moving the cohort default solves it. CON's answer—universal safe defaults—was shown to leave the grade on the same platforms with a toggle a twelve-year-old can flip, and CON's closing claim that minors cannot opt out quietly reintroduced the age gate CON had called catastrophic. PRO also blunted CON's "darker corners" argument with the network point (a grade migrates to Snapchat for the invitations, not to an obscure forum), turning leakage from symmetric to a shrink-the-exposed-population ratio. CON's strongest surviving line was the surveillance asymmetry (liability pushes platforms toward universal ID checks), which PRO only partly answered with reasonable-steps liability and existing age inference; CON also misattributed its own [A4.3] as a PRO concession. Both sides handled the Q/A format properly and both suffered clipping, but PRO's framing ("where does the grade live at twelve?") made the decision easier than CON's shifting scheme.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question forcing CON to choose between a minors-only regime (needing the "catastrophic" gate) and universal defaults (leaky toggle, still exiling the refused child), followed by [B4.6]-[B4.7] and the closing showing that a chronological feed "is still the feed the grade lives on"—CON's coordination answer never recovered.</best_rebuttal>
